How Agile and Scrum Really Work

You start with the problem Agile solves and the four values and twelve principles behind it. Then you learn the Scrum framework exactly as its official guide defines it, and finally how to choose between Scrum, Kanban and a hybrid for a real team.

Picture a team building an online fees portal for a group of private schools in Abuja. In a **plan-driven** project, often called **waterfall**, they gather every requirement in month one, design in month two, build for three months and test at the end. The school owners see nothing usable until month six. If an important assumption was wrong, for example that parents would pay by card when most actually pay by bank transfer or USSD, the team learns it very late, after building the wrong thing.

An **Agile** team works in short cycles, usually one to four weeks. At the end of each cycle they have a small, working piece of the product that real users can try. They show it, collect feedback and adjust the plan. The same wrong assumption is discovered in week two, not month six.

Agile turns one big, distant plan into many small plans that are checked against reality.

In February 2001, seventeen software practitioners met in Snowbird, Utah, USA, and wrote the **Manifesto for Agile Software Development**. It is short. It says they have come to value:

Read the last line of the manifesto carefully: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." Agile does **not** mean no documentation, no plan and no contract. It means those things serve the work, not the other way round. A common misunderstanding in workplaces is to use "we are Agile" as an excuse for no planning at all. That is not Agile, it is chaos.
A few of the twelve principles you will use most
**Deliver working software frequently**, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, preferring the shorter timescale.
**Welcome changing requirements**, even late in development, because change can give the customer an advantage.
**Business people and developers must work together daily** throughout the project.
**Working software is the primary measure of progress.**
**At regular intervals, the team reflects** on how to become more effective, then adjusts its behaviour.
**Simplicity**, the art of maximising the amount of work not done, is essential.
Agile beyond software

The manifesto was written for software, but the same ideas now guide marketing teams, programme teams in NGOs, content studios and event planners. Wherever the work is uncertain and feedback is possible, short cycles help. You will see this applied to non-software teams throughout this course.
Why short cycles work: empiricism

Agile rests on an **empirical** approach: knowledge comes from experience, and decisions are made on what is actually observed. You make a small step, **inspect** the result, and **adapt**. This is the right approach when the work is complex, meaning you cannot know everything in advance. When the work is simple and repeatable, such as printing 500 identical certificates, a fixed plan is perfectly fine.

Worked example: the cost of a late discovery

For example, a team of 4 developers is building the school fees portal. Each developer costs the company about ₦25,000 per working day (approximate, illustrative figure). The card-payment assumption is wrong, and fixing it means rebuilding the payment flow.
Waterfall case: the error is found in testing after 60 working days. Suppose 30% of the work built so far depends on the card assumption. Rework = 30% of 60 days = 18 days for the team.
Agile case: parents try the first working payment screen at the end of sprint 1 (10 working days). Only about 3 days of team work depend on the wrong assumption.
Difference = ₦1,800,000 − ₦300,000 = ₦1,500,000 saved, plus about two months of delay avoided.
Finding the wrong assumption in week two instead of month three cut the rework cost to one sixth. The numbers are illustrative, but the pattern is the core argument for short cycles.
Say it simply
In an interview, a strong one-line answer is: "Agile means delivering value in small, working pieces, checking them with real users often, and changing the plan based on what we learn."

Agile is a set of values. **Scrum** is one specific, lightweight framework that puts those values to work, and it is the most widely used one. It is defined in a free, short document called **The Scrum Guide**, written by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. The current version is from November 2020. Everything in this lesson follows that guide, so you can check it yourself at scrumguides.org.
The Scrum Team: three accountabilities
A Scrum Team is small, **typically 10 or fewer people**, with no sub-teams and no hierarchy inside it. It has three accountabilities (the 2020 guide uses this word instead of "roles"):

Two details are worth remembering. The Product Owner is **one person, not a committee**; others may influence the backlog, but they do it by convincing the Product Owner. And the Scrum Master is a **leader who serves** the team and the wider organisation: coaching, facilitating when asked, and pushing to remove blockers that the team cannot remove alone, such as a slow approval process in another department.
The three pillars and five values

Scrum is built on three pillars: **transparency** (the work and progress are visible to all), **inspection** (the team checks progress often) and **adaptation** (it adjusts as soon as something is off). The guide also names five values: **commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage**. Courage matters more than people expect: it takes courage to say in a review that a feature is not finished.

The three artifacts and their commitments
**Product Backlog**: the ordered list of everything that might improve the product. Its commitment is the **Product Goal**, the long-term objective.
**Sprint Backlog**: the Sprint Goal, the items chosen for this Sprint, and the plan for delivering them. Its commitment is the **Sprint Goal**.

**Increment**: a usable step toward the Product Goal. Its commitment is the **Definition of Done**. Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment and is not shown as finished.

Two more rules are often tested in certification exams. First, **only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint**, and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Second, the 2020 guide no longer prescribes the famous "three questions" for the Daily Scrum: the Developers may use any structure, as long as the meeting focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal.

Scrum is not the only Agile approach, and it is not always the best one. A good practitioner can look at a team's work and say which approach fits. The main alternative you will meet is **Kanban**.
Kanban in one page

Kanban (a Japanese word meaning "signboard") comes from manufacturing and was adapted for knowledge work. It has no Sprints and no fixed roles. Instead, the team makes its work visible on a board, **limits how much work is in progress at once**, and manages the flow of items from start to finish. New work can be pulled in at any time, as soon as there is space.
**Visualise the workflow**: columns such as To do, Doing, Review, Done.
**Limit work in progress (WIP)**: for example, no more than 3 cards in Doing. When the column is full, you finish something before starting something new.
**Measure flow**: how many items finish per day or week (throughput) and how long each takes from start to finish (cycle time).
**Improve continuously**: review the board regularly and remove bottlenecks.
A person moving cards across a progress board
Kanban's main lever is limiting how much is in progress so that work actually finishes.
Little's Law: why WIP limits speed things up

A result from queueing theory called **Little's Law** says that, for a stable system, average cycle time = average work in progress ÷ average throughput. In plain words: if your team finishes the same number of items per day, having more items open at once makes each one take longer.
Worked example: a support team drowning in open tickets
For example, Funmi leads a customer support team at a payments company in Lagos. On average 30 complaint tickets are open, and the team closes about 10 per working day.
Average cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 working days per ticket.
Funmi sets a WIP limit: no more than 15 tickets open in the team at once. New tickets wait in a queue and are pulled in strict priority order.
Closing speed stays about 10 per day, because the team size is unchanged.
New average cycle time = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 working days once a customer's ticket is started.
With less switching between tickets, many teams also find throughput rises a little, which shortens cycle time further.

Halving work in progress halved the time each opened ticket takes. Customers get answers faster without hiring more staff. The queue before the board still needs watching, which is why Funmi also reports total waiting time.

Little's Law only holds when the system is roughly stable, meaning items arrive and leave at about the same rate. If 20 new tickets arrive each day but only 10 are closed, the queue grows every day and no WIP limit can hide that. The honest fix is then a capacity conversation: more people, fewer channels, automated answers to common questions, or a clear statement of what the team will not handle.

Before the first Sprint, a Scrum Team needs three practical things: an ordered **Product Backlog**, a **board** where the Sprint's work is visible, and a written **Definition of Done**. This lesson sets up all three, using a realistic small project.
The Product Backlog: ordered, not just listed

The Product Backlog is owned by the Product Owner. It is a single list, **ordered** by what the Product Owner believes delivers the most value soonest, considering risk, cost and dependencies. Items at the top are small and clear enough to be done within one Sprint. Items lower down can be rough ideas. The Scrum Guide calls the ongoing work of splitting and clarifying items **refinement**.
Each item has a short title, a description of the need, and conditions that show when it is complete.
Items are written as outcomes for a user where possible, not as technical chores.
The order is visible to everyone, so nobody has to guess what comes next.
Refinement usually takes no more than about 10% of the team's time in a Sprint, a common guideline rather than a rule.
Sizing with relative estimates

Scrum does not tell you how to estimate. Many teams use **story points**, a relative size based on effort, complexity and uncertainty, often on the scale 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. A 5 is roughly two to three times a 2. A popular technique is **Planning Poker**: everyone reveals a number at the same time, the highest and lowest explain their thinking, and the team re-votes. The discussion is more valuable than the number, because it exposes hidden work.
A person reviewing an ordered list of tasks
An ordered backlog answers the question "what should we do next?" before anyone has to ask.
Worked example: a first backlog for a bakery ordering service

For example, a 5-person team is building a WhatsApp-based ordering system for Tola's bakery in Ibadan. Tola is the Product Owner. The Product Goal: customers can order and pay for cakes without a phone call.

Brainstorm 9 items, then Tola orders them by value. Top 4: (1) customer sees the cake menu with prices, (2) customer places an order with pickup date, (3) customer pays by bank transfer and uploads proof, (4) Tola gets a daily list of orders.
Refinement: item 3 is too big, so the team splits it into 3a: show bank details and order reference, and 3b: Tola confirms payment and the customer gets a confirmation message.
Planning Poker sizes: item 1 = 3 points, item 2 = 5, item 3a = 2, item 3b = 5, item 4 = 3.
Total for the top five items = 3 + 5 + 2 + 5 + 3 = 18 points.
Lower items (loyalty discount, delivery tracking) stay rough and unsized for now.
The team has a refined, sized top of the backlog worth 18 points, enough for about one Sprint once their real speed is known. Card payment and delivery tracking wait until value is proven.

Protect customer data on boards

Never paste customers' phone numbers, account numbers, BVN or payment screenshots onto a board card. Board tools are shared widely and links get forwarded. The **Definition of Done (DoD)** is a formal description of the quality an Increment must meet. Sprint Planning: why, what, how

Sprint Planning answers three questions from the Scrum Guide. **Why** is this Sprint valuable? The team agrees a **Sprint Goal**, one sentence that gives the Sprint its purpose. **What** can be Done this Sprint? The Developers select items from the top of the backlog. **How** will the work get done? They break items into tasks, often a day or less each. The Developers decide how much they can take on; the Product Owner cannot force more in.
A calendar
Capacity starts with the calendar: holidays, leave and other duties all reduce what fits in a Sprint.
Worked example: capacity and forecast for a 2-week Sprint
For example, Chidi's team has 5 Developers and runs 10-working-day Sprints. One day in this Sprint is a public holiday, and Ada has 2 days of leave. Past Sprints delivered 21, 18 and 24 points.
Available days: 5 people × 10 days = 50 person-days.
Subtract the holiday: 5 × 1 = 5 person-days, so 45 remain.
Subtract Ada's leave: 2 person-days, so 43 remain.
Capacity ratio = 43 ÷ 50 = 0.86, or 86% of a normal Sprint.
Average velocity = (21 + 18 + 24) ÷ 3 = 63 ÷ 3 = 21 points.
Forecast = 21 × 0.86 = 18.06, so about 18 points.

The team forecasts about 18 points, not 21. They pull items worth 18 points from the top of the backlog, write the Sprint Goal "Customers can pay by transfer and get confirmation", and plan tasks for the first few days.

Velocity is a forecast tool, not a target

Velocity (points done per Sprint) is not in the Scrum Guide; it is a common complementary practice. Use it only to forecast your own team. Comparing velocity between teams, or rewarding higher numbers, makes teams inflate their estimates.
The Daily Scrum: 15 minutes, focused on the goal

The Daily Scrum is for the Developers. They look at the board and agree the plan for the next 24 hours toward the Sprint Goal. A useful format is to **walk the board from right to left**: start with items nearest Done and ask what is needed to finish them, then items in progress, then anything blocked. When a topic needs more than a minute, the Scrum Master says "let's take that after" and notes it. Those who need to stay remain for the follow-up; everyone else goes back to work.

For remote teams, keep the board on screen and let one Developer share it while others speak. On weak connections, switch cameras off and keep audio only. Start on time even if one person is late; the Daily Scrum belongs to those present.
The Sprint Review: a working session, not a slideshow
Product Owner restates the Sprint Goal and what was and was not Done (5 minutes).
Developers demonstrate the working Increment on a real device, ideally with a stakeholder using it (30 to 40 minutes).
Stakeholders give feedback; the Product Owner notes new or changed backlog items (30 minutes).
Group looks at what has changed in the market, budget or timeline, and discusses what to do next (20 minutes).

Invite the people who will use or pay for the product, not only managers. Ask open questions such as "what would stop you using this tomorrow?" rather than "do you like it?". Never demo work that is not Done; show it as in progress or leave it out.

Many organisations perform Scrum events without getting Scrum's benefits. People call this **"Scrum in name only"** or cargo-cult Scrum. Your job, especially as a Scrum Master, is to notice the warning signs early, using data and honest conversation, not blame.
Reading a burndown chart

A **Sprint burndown chart** plots the work remaining (in points, tasks or hours) against the days of the Sprint. An **ideal line** runs straight from the total on day 0 to zero on the last day. The **actual line** shows reality. Burndowns are not required by Scrum, but they are a simple, popular way to make progress transparent.
A chart with a line trending downward
A healthy burndown slopes down steadily; a flat line in the first half of the Sprint is a signal to act.
Worked example: spotting trouble on day 5
For example, Halima's team planned 40 points in a 10-day Sprint. On the evening of day 5 the chart shows 34 points remaining.
Ideal burn rate = 40 ÷ 10 = 4 points per day.
Ideal remaining at day 5 = 40 − (5 × 4) = 20 points.
Actual remaining = 34 points, so the team is 34 − 20 = 14 points behind the ideal line.
Actual rate so far = (40 − 34) ÷ 5 = 1.2 points per day. At that rate, the last 5 days would finish only 6 more points, leaving 28 undone.
At the next Daily Scrum, Halima asks what is blocking work. The team finds three items all waiting for one API key from a partner bank.
The Developers and Product Owner agree to escalate the key that morning, and the Product Owner renegotiates scope: an 8-point item that does not serve the Sprint Goal goes back to the backlog.

The chart did not fix anything by itself; it started the right conversation on day 5 instead of day 10. Scope was adjusted with the Product Owner while keeping the Sprint Goal, which the Scrum Guide allows.

Whether you are joining a team as Scrum Master or invited in as a coach, your first job is not to teach Scrum. It is to **understand what is really happening**. Teams that say "Scrum does not work here" are often running a version with key parts missing. Teams that say "we do Scrum perfectly" sometimes hide serious problems. Discovery gives you evidence before you suggest anything.

Ask the same questions to several people separately: the Product Owner, two or three Developers, and the manager who sponsors the team. Differences between their answers are often the most useful finding. Observe at least one Daily Scrum and one Review or Retrospective in person or on the call, without speaking.
**When observing a Daily Scrum**, note the start and end times, who speaks most, whether the Sprint Goal is mentioned, and whether anyone reports to a manager rather than to the team.
**When observing a Review**, note whether real users attend, whether working product is shown, and whether the backlog changes as a result.
**When looking at the board**, count items in progress per person and items older than one Sprint.
**Write facts, not judgements**: "Daily Scrum lasted 34 minutes; the manager asked each person for status" rather than "the meeting was bad".

Harvard professor Amy Edmondson describes psychological safety as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as admitting mistakes or asking questions. During discovery, promise that individual comments will not be quoted with names, and keep that promise.

After the interviews, run a 45-minute health check with the whole team. Each person scores eight statements from 1 (not true at all) to 5 (completely true), anonymously, for example with a Google Form. You then show the averages and discuss the lowest two.

For example, a 7-person programme team at a women's empowerment NGO in Enugu plans and delivers online training cohorts in 2-week Sprints. Kemi, their new Scrum Master, runs the health check. All 7 respond.

Statement 2 (Product Owner available) scores: 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 1. Total = 13. Average = 13 ÷ 7 = 1.86.
Statement 8 (safe to raise problems) averages 4.3, so safety is not the main issue.
Interviews explain the low scores: the programme director, who is Product Owner, is often travelling, and donors' requests go straight to individual staff.
With the team, Kemi agrees two experiments for the next two Sprints: a named deputy who can answer day-to-day questions, and a rule that all new requests go onto the backlog first.
Success measure: both averages rise above 3 at the next health check in four weeks.

The team works on two specific, measured problems instead of "doing Scrum better" in general. The lowest scores pointed straight at the cause: decisions and incoming work were not flowing through the Product Owner.

Setting a day rate you can live on

Independent consultants are not paid for every working day. Time goes to finding clients, preparing training, travel, invoicing and learning. A simple way to set a rate is: monthly income you need (including tax, pension, data, transport and tools) ÷ the number of days you can realistically bill in a month. If you need ₦1,000,000 a month and can bill about 12 days, your floor is about ₦83,000 per day. Then check it against what similar roles earn locally and what value the client expects. Never price from guesswork alone; ask peers, read job adverts and keep records of what clients accept.
What a short proposal contains
**Situation**: two or three sentences from your discovery, in the client's own words where possible.
**Outcomes**: what will be different, with measures (for example, Sprint Goals met in at least 3 of the last 4 Sprints).
**Activities**: exactly what you will do, how often and with whom.
**Exclusions**: what is not included (for example, coaching additional teams, writing software, HR decisions).
**Duration and review points**: start date, end date, and a mid-point review.
**Fees and payment terms**: amount, schedule, and how changes are handled.
Worked example: fixed package or retainer?

For example, Ifeoma is an experienced Scrum Master. A Port Harcourt software firm wants help for one team. She decides her day rate from her own costs and income target; here we use ₦80,000 per day as an illustrative figure, not a market rate.
Option A, fixed kick-off package: 3 days discovery and health check + 2 days training + 4 half-days supporting events = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 days. Fee = 7 × ₦80,000 = ₦560,000.
Option B, part-time Scrum Master for 3 months at 2 days per week: about 2 × 4 = 8 days a month. Monthly retainer = 8 × ₦80,000 = ₦640,000. Three months = ₦1,920,000.
She offers Option B at a small commitment discount of 10% for paying monthly in advance: ₦640,000 × 0.9 = ₦576,000 per month, ₦1,728,000 in total.
Halfway through, the client asks her to add a second team. Her change note: 1 extra day per week for the remaining 6 weeks = 6 days × ₦80,000 = ₦480,000, with a revised end-of-engagement review.
The client signs the change note before the extra work starts.
Both options and the change are priced from the same day rate, so the client can compare them easily. The written change note means the second team is extra paid work, not free scope creep.

Payment and scam safety

Use a written agreement and invoices for every engagement. Request a deposit before starting for new clients. Be wary of overseas "clients" who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference, or who ask you to pay for software or training before they hire you; these are known scam patterns. Receive payments through your business bank account or a recognised processor such as Paystack.
**Name the decision-maker**: one client contact who can approve change notes and sign off milestones.
**Agree how you will measure success** before you start, using numbers from your health check.
**Plan your exit**: from the first month, train someone inside the team to carry on, so the client does not depend on you forever.
**Keep a short weekly note** of what you did and what changed; it supports your invoice and your portfolio.

Finally, be honest about what Scrum can and cannot fix. If the real problem is that leadership sets fixed scope and fixed dates without listening to the team, say so early. A good coach protects the client's money by naming the real constraint, even when it is uncomfortable.

Read the Scrum Guide slowly, twice. It is short, and most exam questions test its exact wording, such as "accountabilities", "commitments" and who owns which decision.

Your evidence portfolio

You already have material from this course: a Sprint calendar, a backlog and board, a mini-Sprint with a burndown, a Retrospective action log, a health check and a proposal. Turn the best of it into a **one-page case study** using this structure:
**Context**: team, product or programme, and your role (be honest if it was a practice or volunteer project).
**Problem**: what was not working, with a number if you have one.
**What you did**: the Scrum practices you introduced or facilitated.
**Result**: what changed, with before-and-after numbers.
**What you learned**: one thing you would do differently.
Worked example: case study numbers from a volunteer team
For example, Zainab volunteers with a church youth unit that runs a monthly outreach event. She introduced 2-week Sprints, a Trello board and Retrospectives for three months.
Before: over the 3 events before Scrum, 21 tasks were planned and 12 were done on time. On-time rate = 12 ÷ 21 = 57%.
After: over the next 3 events, 24 tasks were planned and 20 were done on time. On-time rate = 20 ÷ 24 = 83%.
Improvement = 83 − 57 = 26 percentage points.
Retrospective actions: 6 agreed, 5 completed, so 5 ÷ 6 = 83% followed through.
Her case study headline: "Raised on-time task completion from 57% to 83% in three months by introducing Sprints, a visible board and action-focused Retrospectives."
A volunteer project with honest, simple numbers gives an interviewer something concrete to ask about, which is far stronger than listing "knowledge of Scrum" on a CV.

"The Daily Scrum always runs 40 minutes. How would you fix it?" (Walk the board; move problem-solving after; check who is attending and why.)
"Your team's velocity dropped by a third. What does that tell you?" (Nothing by itself; look at capacity, item size, blockers and quality before judging.)
"What is the difference between Agile and Scrum?" (Values and principles versus one framework that applies them.)

Why Agile
Agile

Picture a team building a school fees portal in Abuja. In a plan-driven project, often called waterfall, they gather every requirement first, build for months, and test at the end. The school owners see nothing usable until month six.
An Agile team works in short cycles of 1 to 4 weeks. Each cycle ends with a small working piece that real users can try. They collect feedback and adjust the plan.
Agile does not mean no plan. Both approaches plan. The difference is how often the plan meets reality.
Worked example
The cost of a late discovery
For example, 4 developers build the fees portal. Each costs about ₦25,000 per working day.
Team cost per day
Waterfall rework, 18 days
Agile rework, 3 days
Illustrative, approximate figures.
The team assumed parents would pay by card. Most actually pay by bank transfer or USSD.
With 4 developers at about 25,000 naira a day, the team costs 100,000 naira a day.
In waterfall, the error appears in testing after 60 days. 30% of the work depends on it, so 18 days must be redone. That is 1,800,000 naira.
In Agile, parents try the first payment screen after sprint 1. Only about 3 days of work depend on the wrong idea. That is 300,000 naira.
One sixth of the cost, and about two months of delay avoided. That is the core argument for short cycles: inspect what really happened, then adapt.
The Scrum Team
Three accountabilities
One person, not a committee. Maximises value and orders the Product Backlog.
A leader who serves: coaches, facilitates, removes blockers. Not a task manager.
Create a usable Increment every Sprint. Testers, designers and writers count too.

Scrum is the most used framework for putting Agile to work. It is defined in the free Scrum Guide, last updated in November 2020. A Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer people, with three accountabilities.
The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. She maximises value and orders the Product Backlog.
The Scrum Master is a leader who serves. She coaches and removes blockers. A common mistake is acting as a task manager who assigns work.
The Developers create a usable Increment every Sprint. Developer does not mean only programmers. Testers, designers and writers are Developers too.
Five events
A 2-week Sprint, event by event
The Sprint: 2 weeks, fixed length
Sprint Planning: about 4 hours
Daily Scrum: 15 minutes, every day
Sprint Review: about 2 hours
Sprint Retrospective: about 1.5 hours
A timebox is a maximum duration. The Sprint holds all the other events. Many teams use 2 weeks, which is 10 working days.
Sprint Planning decides why this Sprint is valuable and what can be done. About 4 hours for 2 weeks.
The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes every working day. Developers check progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust the plan.
The Sprint Review inspects the result with stakeholders, and the Retrospective plans how to work better.
For example, Amaka's team spends 10 hours per person on events out of about 80. That is 12.5%. Useful when a manager asks, why so many meetings?
Kanban in four practices
Visualise the work on a board
Limit work in progress
Measure throughput and cycle time
Improve continuously
When Doing is full, finish something before starting more.
Kanban has no Sprints and no fixed roles. First, show the work on a board with columns like To do, Doing, Review, Done.
Second, limit work in progress. For example, no more than 3 cards in Doing. When the column is full, finish something first.
Third, measure flow. Little's Law says cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput.
For example, Funmi's support team has 30 tickets open and closes 10 a day. That is 3 days per ticket. She limits open tickets to 15, so each started ticket takes 1.5 days.
Fourth, review the board and remove bottlenecks. But if 20 tickets arrive a day and only 10 close, no limit can hide that. Have an honest capacity conversation.
Choose wisely
Which approach fits the work?
New app or website: Scrum
Help desk or support: Kanban
Borehole to a known design: plan-driven
Campaigns plus urgent work: hybrid
Match the approach to the work. A new app suits Scrum, because the solution is uncertain. A help desk suits Kanban, because work arrives every hour.
A borehole to a known design suits a fixed plan. Campaigns plus urgent requests suit a hybrid.
If urgent work broke the plan almost every week last month, choose Kanban or keep capacity free.

To remember. Agile means small working pieces, checked with real users often. Late discovery costs far more than early.
Scrum has a Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers. The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes. And lower work in progress means faster finishing.

Why this matters
Knowing the events is not enough
An ordered, sized Product Backlog

Early warning when a Sprint drifts
Many teams perform the Scrum events without getting the benefits. Running Scrum well starts with an ordered backlog and an honest forecast.
Then a clear Definition of Done protects quality, and a simple chart warns you early when a Sprint is drifting. Let us walk through each one.
Product Backlog
Tola's bakery ordering backlog
One list, ordered by value
Top items small enough for one Sprint
Split items that are too big
Size with Planning Poker
Top five items: 18 points

For example, a 5-person team is building a WhatsApp ordering system for Tola's bakery in Ibadan. Tola is the Product Owner. She orders the backlog by value: first the menu with prices, then placing an order, then paying by transfer.
Items at the top must be small and clear enough to finish in one Sprint. Lower items can stay rough ideas.
Paying by transfer is too big, so the team splits it in two: show bank details and an order reference, then Tola confirms payment.
They size items with Planning Poker. Everyone shows a number at once, on a scale like 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. The highest and lowest explain, and the team votes again. The talk exposes hidden work.
The top five items total 3, 5, 2, 5 and 3. That is 18 points.
Forecast from real capacity
5 people x 10 days = 50 person-days
Minus a holiday: 5, leaves 45
Minus Ada's leave: 2, leaves 43
Capacity: 43 ÷ 50 = 86%
Average velocity: 63 ÷ 3 = 21 points
Forecast: 21 x 0.86 = about 18
The Developers decide how much they take on.
For example, Chidi's team has 5 Developers in a 10-day Sprint. That is 50 person-days.
One day is a public holiday, which removes 5. Ada has 2 days of leave. That leaves 43.
43 divided by 50 is 86% of a normal Sprint.
Their last three Sprints delivered 21, 18 and 24 points. The average, called velocity, is 21.
So the forecast is 21 times 0.86, about 18 points, not 21. The Product Owner cannot force more in.
Use velocity only to forecast your own team. Never compare or reward it between teams, or estimates inflate.
Sprint Goal
Weak goal versus strong goal
Weak
Strong
Customers pay by transfer, get confirmed
Director sees weekly sales on her phone
Sprint Planning also produces one Sprint Goal. Finish tickets 14 to 22 is weak. It names work, not value.
Customers can pay by transfer and get confirmation is strong. It names a user and a checkable result, so the team can swap items and still meet it.
Definition of Done
Tola's Definition of Done
Works on a low-cost Android on slow 3G
Tested by someone other than the builder
No customer personal data in logs
Wording checked by the Product Owner
How-to note updated
The Definition of Done is the quality bar. If an item misses it, it is not shown as done. It goes back to the backlog.
Keep it short and checkable. Five honest checks beat twenty that nobody follows.
And never put phone numbers, BVN or payment screenshots on a board card. Use an order reference, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.
Burndown chart
Halima spots trouble on day 5
40 points over 10 days is 4 a day. By day 5, 20 points should remain.
34 points remain: 14 behind. At 1.2 a day, 28 points would be left undone.
Three items wait for one API key. Escalate it, and move an 8-point item back to the backlog.
A burndown chart plots the work remaining against the days. For example, Halima's team planned 40 points in a 10-day Sprint. That is 4 points a day, so by day 5, 20 should remain.
But 34 remain. They are 14 points behind. At their pace, 28 points would be left undone.

At the next Daily Scrum, she asks what is blocking work. Three items wait for one API key from a partner bank. They escalate it that morning, and the Product Owner moves an 8-point item back to the backlog, while keeping the Sprint Goal.
The chart fixed nothing alone. It started the right talk on day 5 instead of day 10.
Key points
Remember
Order the backlog; split big items
Forecast with velocity adjusted for capacity
Daily Scrum is 15 minutes; solve problems after
Done means it meets the Definition of Done
End each Retrospective with one or two actions
To remember. Order the backlog and split big items. Forecast with velocity adjusted for real capacity. Keep the Daily Scrum to 15 minutes and solve problems after it.
Done means it meets the Definition of Done. And end every Retrospective with one or two actions, each with an owner and a date.

Why this matters
Understand before you teach
Find out what is really happening
Turn opinions into numbers
Price and protect your scope
Show honest evidence
When you join a team as Scrum Master or coach, your first job is not to teach Scrum. It is to understand what is really happening, and to measure it.
Then you scope and price your work so it is protected, and you build honest evidence that employers and clients can trust.
Discovery
Process: your last Sprint, start to finish
People: when was a problem last raised?
Tools and data: show me your board
Leadership: who can add work to the team?
Ask about process. Walk me through your last Sprint. What was the Sprint Goal? Was it met?
Ask about people. When did someone last raise a problem in a Retrospective, and what happened next? Listen for fear, silence or blame.
Ask to see the board. When was it last updated?
And ask who can add work, and how deadlines are set.
Ask several people separately, then watch a real Daily Scrum without speaking. Write facts, not judgements: the Daily Scrum lasted 34 minutes, not the meeting was bad.
Health check
Kemi scores her team from 1 to 5
Seven anonymous scores total 15. Average: 15 ÷ 7 = 2.14.
Scores total 13. Average: 1.86, the lowest of all.
A named deputy answers daily questions; all new requests go onto the backlog first.

Next, a scored health check. For example, Kemi is the new Scrum Master for a 7-person NGO training team in Enugu. Everyone scores eight statements from 1 to 5, anonymously, in a Google Form. We finish what we start averages just 2.14.

Our Product Owner is available averages 1.86. Feeling safe to raise problems averages 4.3, so safety is not the issue. Interviews show the director is often travelling, and donor requests go straight to staff.

With the team, Kemi agrees two experiments: a named deputy for daily questions, and all new requests go onto the backlog first. Success means both averages rise above 3 in four weeks. Share patterns, never names.
Worked example
Ifeoma prices two options
For example, Ifeoma, an experienced Scrum Master, uses an illustrative day rate of ₦80,000.
Option A: kick-off, 7 days
Option B: per month, 8 days
Option B with 10% discount
Change note: second team
Illustrative figures, not a market rate.
To set a day rate, divide the monthly income you need by the days you can really bill. For example, 1,000,000 naira over about 12 days gives a floor of about 83,000 naira a day.
Ifeoma uses 80,000 naira a day, as an illustration.
Option A is a 7-day kick-off package: 560,000 naira.
Option B is a part-time Scrum Master role, 8 days a month: 640,000 naira. With 10% off for paying monthly in advance, it is 576,000.
Midway, the client wants a second team added. Her change note: 6 extra days, 480,000 naira, signed before the work starts. That is paid work, not free scope creep.
Your proposal
Situation, in the client's words
Outcomes with measures
Activities: what, how often, with whom
Exclusions
Duration and a mid-point review
Fees, payment terms, change handling
Your proposal states the situation, measurable outcomes, exactly what you will do, and what is excluded, like coaching a second team.
It gives dates with a mid-point review, and fees, payment terms and how changes are handled. Writing exclusions down is what makes a change note possible later.
Protect your money
Safe payments, known scams
Do
Written agreement and invoices
Deposit from new clients
Business account or Paystack
Pay only on official sites
Beware
Overpay, then ask for a refund
Pay for training before hiring
Guaranteed job after a certificate
Exam dumps, personal accounts

Use a written agreement and invoices for every job, take a deposit from new clients, and receive payments through your business account or a processor like Paystack. Pay for certificates only on the official sites.

Be wary of clients who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference, or who ask you to pay for software or training before they hire you. Avoid anyone who guarantees a job, sells exam dumps, or wants payment to a personal account.
Prepare for a Scrum assessment
Read the Scrum Guide slowly, twice
Summarise each section in one line
Repeat free practice tests
Watch for must, always and only
Quiz each other in a study group
If the Scrum Guide does not say it, Scrum does not require it.
PSM I needs only an online assessment. CSM needs a course with a Certified Scrum Trainer. Always check current fees on the official sites. To prepare, read the Scrum Guide slowly, twice.
Write one line per section, then take the free practice tests until you score well every time, reading every explanation.
Watch for trick words like must, always and only. And quiz each other in a small WhatsApp study group.
Key points
Remember
Interview, observe, then measure
Fix the lowest two areas with experiments
Price every option from one day rate
Signed change notes control scope
Honest numbers beat buzzwords
To remember. Interview, observe, then measure. Work on the lowest two areas with measured experiments. Price every option from one day rate, and control scope with signed change notes.
And show honest numbers. For example, Zainab's church youth unit raised on-time tasks from 57% to 83%. That beats any buzzword on a CV.
